collection.title: The Bern Sleep-Wake Registry: A 25-year multimodal resource for data-driven sleep medicine
collection.authors: van der Meer, J.; Filchenko, I.; Brill, A.-K.; Wenz, E.; Fregolente, L.; Zub, K.; Dietmann, A.; Schaefer, C.; Roethlisberger, S. C.; Helmy, A.; Tzovara, A.; Fiorillo, L.; Faraci, F. D.; Valenzuela, W.; Schindler, K. A.; Schmitt, W.; Schmidt, M. H.; Bassetti, C. L. A.
collection.author_corresponding_institution: Sleep-Wake Epilepsy Center, Department of Neurology, Inselspital, University Hospital Bern, University of Bern, Bern, Switzerland
collection.abstract:
BackgroundSleep-wake-circadian disorders are prevalent and contribute substantially to morbidity, mortality and reduced quality of life. Evaluation in real-world settings is essential to capture their complexity and association with long-term outcomes. Most sleep-wake registries are restricted to selected populations, lack systematic integration of objective sleep-wake-circadian assessments with the clinical data and provide limited follow-up. To address these limitations, we established the Bern Sleep-Wake Registry based on real-world data from a tertiary University Hospital sleep center.

MethodsThe registry includes data from patients referred to the multidisciplinary Sleep-Center at Inselspital, University Hospital Bern (founded in 1990), from the year 2000 onwards who underwent at least one objective assessment such as polysomnography, daytime sleep-wake recordings, vigilance tests, and actigraphy. The registry integrates clinical information, questionnaire scores, outputs of objective assessments and raw signal data, and is regularly updated to incorporate new patients and longitudinal follow-up information.

ResultsAs of September 2025, records from over 11000 patients were evaluated (median age: 50 years (interquartile range 36, 61); 65% male). The most common sleep-wake-circadian disorders were "sleep-related breathing disorders" (67%), "insomnia disorders" (15%) and "central disorders of hypersomnolence" (9%). Available assessments included more than 12000 polysomnographies, 2400 multiple sleep latency tests, 2100 maintenance of wakefulness tests, 1800 vigilance tests and 4500 actigraphies.

ConclusionsBy longitudinally integrating multimodal deep clinical phenotyping with objective assessments and raw physiological signals, the Bern Sleep-Wake Registry provides a foundation for investigating disease trajectories, identifying novel biomarkers and developing data-driven approaches to precise diagnosis, prognosis and individualized treatment.

collection.title: AI-Assisted Tissue-Based Antibody Interpretation in Autoimmune Encephalitis: Prospective Validation and Reader Study
collection.authors: Cao, Z.; Xie, D.; Zou, S.; Li, D.; Martinez-Martinez, P.; Zong, S.; Zhang, Z.
collection.abstract:
Tissue-based assays provide broad screening for neural autoantibodies but remain vulnerable to technical and reader-dependent variability. We evaluated an integrated workflow combining automated 3,3'-diaminobenzidine tissue-based assay processing, digital whole-slide imaging, and interpretable deep learning. Model development used 2,357 retrospective serum and cerebrospinal fluid images referred from more than 80 institutions and processed in a centralized laboratory, with reference labels established by expert-consensus tissue-based assay interpretation. A prospective validation cohort included 200 images from 200 unique patients (154 positive and 46 negative; 100 serum and 100 cerebrospinal fluid). The same images were evaluated by two expert and two novice readers in a fixed-order two-round study, with unaided interpretation followed by artificial-intelligence-assisted interpretation after a washout of at least two weeks. The standalone binary classifier achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.922, accuracy of 86.5%, sensitivity of 85.7%, and specificity of 89.1% in prospective validation. Pooled reader accuracy was 90.4% in the unaided round and 97.4% in the artificial-intelligence-assisted round (McNemar P < 0.001), with specificity of 82.6% and 99.5%, respectively. Novice-reader accuracy was 83.3% unaided and 96.5% with artificial-intelligence assistance (P < 0.001), approaching unaided expert accuracy of 97.5%. Among tissue-based-assay-positive cases, reader accuracy for cytoplasmic/nuclear antigen-associated versus neural surface antigen-associated staining-pattern subclassification was 88.8% unaided and 94.0% with artificial-intelligence assistance (P < 0.001). These findings support further multicentre, cross-platform evaluation of artificial-intelligence-assisted neural autoantibody tissue interpretation.

Abbreviated summaryCao et al. report prospective validation of an automated tissue-based neural autoantibody workflow combining digital imaging and interpretable deep learning. Artificial-intelligence-assisted reading was associated with higher interpretation accuracy, particularly among less-experienced readers, supporting further multicentre validation across laboratories and imaging platforms.

collection.title: Prospective validation of an uncertainty-aware machine learning model for secondary progressive multiple sclerosis classification
collection.authors: Parakkal Sreenivasan, A.; Noui, Y.; Erngren, I.; Spjuth, O.; Burman, J.; Kultima, K.
collection.abstract:
BackgroundRelapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS) often progresses to secondary-progressive MS (SPMS), but diagnosis is typically retrospective, delaying potential interventions. Existing rule-based and machine learning approaches often lack prospective validation and provide no uncertainty estimates, limiting clinical adoption.

ObjectiveTo prospectively evaluate a conformal prediction (CP)-enabled random forest model for reproducing clinician-recorded disease course labels in the Swedish Multiple Sclerosis Registry (SMSReg) and compare its classifications with the Lorscheider criteria.

MethodsThe CP model was trained and calibrated on SMSReg-2022 (10,787 individuals, 85,461 hospital visits) and then validated on SMSReg-2025 (15,719 individuals, 45,077 hospital visits; not included in the SMSReg-2022 training/calibration/testing datasets). Performance was assessed at the hospital visit and individual levels and compared with the Lorscheider criteria.

ResultsThe model maintained good calibration on the prospective dataset. At the per-hospital visit-level, the model accuracies were 92% (RRMS) and 95% (SPMS). At the individual level, sensitivity was 98%, specificity 89%, and F1-score 0.75. With clinician-recorded labels as reference, the model showed higher sensitivity than the Lorscheider criteria (98% vs. 71%), more transition assignments (90% vs. 57%), and higher F1-score (0.76 vs. 0.69).

ConclusionThe CP-enabled model prospectively reproduced clinician-recorded disease course labels with calibrated uncertainty, supporting harmonization and decision support.

collection.title: Clinical utility of plasma APOE proteotyping for Alzheimer's disease risk and prognosis
collection.authors: Shi, R.; Choity, L. T.; Farinas, M. F.; Zeng, X.; Emanuel, J. E.; Saeed, A.; Reis, S. E.; Lopez, O. L.; Kamboh, M. I.; Cohen, A. D.; Gildengers, A. G.; Wilckens, K. A.; Karikari, T. K.
collection.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Psychiatry, School of Medicine, University of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, PA USA
collection.abstract:
BackgroundAlzheimers disease (AD) is a complex neurodegenerative disorder strongly influenced by genetic factors, with apolipoprotein E (APOE) {varepsilon}4 allele being the most established risk variant. Although DNA-based genotyping remains standard, plasma proteotyping may provide scalable, isoform-specific alternatives. Here, we aimed to investigate the clinical utility of APOE proteotyping as a surrogate for genotyping in different clinical and research cohorts.

MethodsPlasma APOE4 protein were quantified using the NULISAseq CNS panel across four cohorts (ADRC, HeartSCORE, LATTICE, and ALPS). DNA-based APOE genotyping was the reference standard. Proteotyping thresholds for APOE {varepsilon}4 carrier status and copy number were derived in ADRC and externally validated in the other cohorts. Logistic, proportional-odds, and Cox proportional-hazards models compared genotype- and proteotype-defined groups in relation to amyloid positivity, cross-sectional CDR global scores, and time to CDR-SB worsening, respectively.

ResultsPlasma APOE4 accurately classified APOE {varepsilon}4 carrier status in ADRC (AUC=0.977, 95%CI 0.967-0.985; threshold 5.78 NULISA protein quantification [NPQ] value) and achieved near-perfect external validation in HeartSCORE, LATTICE, and ALPS (all AUCs=1.000, 95%CI 1.000-1.000). Plasma APOE4 also well-differentiated heterozygous from homozygous {varepsilon}4 carriers (ADRC AUC=0.879, 95%CI 0.834-0.921; threshold 12.23 NPQ value). Genotype- and proteotype-defined {varepsilon}4 carrier status showed similar associations with amyloid positivity (OR=4.40 vs 4.45), higher CDR global scores (OR=1.50 for both), and CDR-SB worsening (HR=1.22 for both).

DiscussionPlasma APOE4 proteotyping accurately distinguished genotype-defined APOE {varepsilon}4 carrier status and copy number while demonstrating AD-related associations comparable to DNA genotyping.
